# Diferential Calculus

This chapter is devoted to diferential calculus. Tools from diferential calculus are widely used in many branches of analysis, including in optimization. In optimization, our main concern in this book, they are used, among other things, to derive optimality conditions in extremal problems which are described by diferentiable functions. 

We treat the calculus of scalar-valued functions $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ or vectorvalued functions (maps) $f : U \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , where U is an open set in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . The vector spaces $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ and $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ can replaced with any finite-dimensional vector spaces over R without changing any of our results or methods. In fact, most of our results remain true (with some minor changes) if $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ and $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ are replaced by Banach spaces. Although this extension can be done in a straightforward manner, we desire to keep our presentation fairly concrete, and the finite-dimensional vector space setting is suficient for our needs. We deviate from this rule only in Chapter 3, where we consider diferentiable functions in Banach spaces. 

The interested reader is referred to the books by Edwards [84] and Spivak [245] for more detailed treatments of calculus in finite-dimensional vector spaces, and Dieudonn´e [77] and H¨ormander [140] in Banach spaces. Surveys of diferential calculus in even more general vector spaces may be found in the references [11, 12]. 

## 1.1 Taylor’s Formula

Taylor’s formula in one or several variables is needed to obtain necessary and suficient conditions for local optimal solutions to unconstrained and constrained optimization problems. In this section, we treat Taylor’s formula for functions of a single variable. The several-variable version of the formula is treated in later sections of this chapter. 

We start with Taylor’s formula in Lagrange’s form. 

Theorem 1.1. Let $f : I = ( c , d ) \to \mathbb { R }$ be a n-times diferentiable function. If $a , b$ are distinct points in I, then there exists a point x strictly between a and b such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (b) = f (a) + f ^ {\prime} (a) (b - a) + \frac {f ^ {\prime \prime} (a)}{2} (b - a) ^ {2} + \dots + \frac {f ^ {(n - 1)} (a)}{(n - 1) !} (b - a) ^ {n - 1} \\ \qquad + \frac {f ^ {(n)} (\overline {{x}})}{n !} (b - a) ^ {n} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {n - 1} \frac {f ^ {(i)} (a)}{i !} (b - a) ^ {i} + \frac {f ^ {(n)} (\overline {{x}})}{n !} (b - a) ^ {n}. \end{array}
$$

Note that the case $n = 1$ is precisely the mean value theorem. 

Proof. The idea of the proof is similar to that in the case $n = 1$ : create a function $g ( t )$ such that $g ^ { ( k ) } ( a ) = 0 , k = 0 , \ldots , n - 1 , g ( b ) = 0$ , and apply Rolle’s theorem repeatedly. 

The (n 1)th-degree Taylor approximation (polynomial) at $a ,$ 

$$
P _ {n - 1} (t) = f (a) + f ^ {\prime} (a) (t - a) + \frac {f ^ {\prime \prime} (a)}{2} (t - a) ^ {2} + \dots + \frac {f ^ {(n - 1)} (a)}{(n - 1) !} (t - a) ^ {n - 1},
$$

satisfies the conditions $P _ { n - 1 } ^ { ( k ) } ( a ) = f ^ { ( k ) } ( a ) , k = 0 , \dots , n - 1$ . Thus, the function $h ( t ) : = f ( t ) - P _ { n - 1 } ( t )$ satisfies the condition $h ^ { ( k ) } ( a ) = 0 , k = 0 , \ldots , n - 1$ However, $h ( b )$ may not vanish. We rectify the situation by defining 

$$
g (t) = f (t) - P _ {n - 1} (t) - \frac {K}{n !} (t - a) ^ {n},
$$

with the constant K chosen such that $g ( b ) = 0$ , that is, 

$$
f (b) = P _ {n - 1} (b) + \frac {K}{n !} (b - a) ^ {n}.\tag{1.1}
$$

Then, 

$$
g ^ {(k)} (a) = f ^ {(k)} (a) - P _ {n - 1} ^ {(k)} (a) = 0, \quad k = 0, \dots , n - 1, \qquad g (b) = 0.
$$

Rolle’s theorem implies that there exists $x _ { 1 }$ strictly between $a$ and b such that $g ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 1 } ) = 0$ . Since $g ^ { \prime } ( a ) = g ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 1 } ) = 0$ , Rolle’s theorem applied to $g ^ { \prime }$ implies that there exists $x _ { 2 }$ strictly between $a$ and $x _ { 1 }$ such that $g ^ { \prime \prime } ( x _ { 2 } ) = 0$ We continue in this fashion and obtain $\{ x _ { i } \} _ { 1 } ^ { n - 1 }$ such that $g ^ { ( i - 1 ) } \bar { ( } x _ { i - 1 } \bar { ) } = 0$ Finally, $g ^ { ( n - 1 ) } ( a ) = g ^ { ( n - 1 ) } ( x _ { n - 1 } ) = 0$ , and applying Rolle’s theorem once more, we obtain a point $x _ { n }$ strictly between a and $x _ { n - 1 }$ such that $g ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { n } ) = 0$ Since $g ^ { ( n ) } ( t ) = f ^ { ( { \bar { n } } ) } ( t ) - K$ , we have $g ^ { ( n ) } ( x _ { n } ) = K$ . Equation (1.1) implies the theorem. □ 

This proof is adapted from [268]. 

In practice, the most useful cases of Taylor’s theorem correspond to $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ 

Corollary 1.2. Let f : $I = ( c , d ) \to \mathbb { R }$ be a function and a, b be distinct points in I. 

(i) (Mean value theorem) If f is diferentiable on I, then there exists a point $\xi$ strictly between a and b such that 

$$
f (b) = f (a) + f ^ {\prime} (\xi) (b - a).
$$

(ii) If f is twice diferentiable on I, then there exists a point ζ strictly between a and b such that 

$$
f (b) = f (a) + f ^ {\prime} (a) (b - a) + \frac {f ^ {\prime \prime} (\zeta)}{2} (b - a) ^ {2}.
$$

Another form of Taylor’s theorem expresses the remainder term as an iterated integral. Its proof is perhaps conceptually the simplest, and it can be used to easily deduce other forms of Taylor’s theorem from it. 

Theorem 1.3. Let f satisfy the conditions of Theorem 1.1. We have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (b) = f (a) + f ^ {\prime} (a) (b - a) + \frac {f ^ {\prime \prime} (a)}{2 !} (b - a) ^ {2} + \dots \\ \qquad + \frac {f ^ {(n - 1)} (a)}{(n - 1) !} (b - a) ^ {n - 1} + \int_ {a} ^ {b} \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {1}} \dots \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {n - 1}} f ^ {(n)} (s _ {n}) d s _ {n} \dots d s _ {1}. \end{array}\tag{1.2}
$$

Proof. The idea of the proof is to use the fundamental theorem of calculus repeatedly. First, we have $\textstyle f ( b ) - f ( a ) = \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ^ { \prime } ( x ) d x$ , or 

$$
f (b) = f (a) + \int_ {a} ^ {b} f ^ {\prime} (s _ {1}) d s _ {1}.
$$

Similarly, $\begin{array} { r } { f ^ { \prime } ( s _ { 1 } ) = f ^ { \prime } ( a ) + \int _ { a } ^ { s _ { 1 } } f ^ { \prime \prime } ( s _ { 2 } ) d s _ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , and this gives 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (b) = f (a) + \int_ {a} ^ {b} f ^ {\prime} (s _ {1}) d s _ {1} = f (a) + \int_ {a} ^ {b} \left(f ^ {\prime} (a) + \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {1}} f ^ {\prime \prime} (s _ {2}) d s _ {2}\right) d s _ {1} \\ = f (a) + f ^ {\prime} (a) (b - a) + \int_ {a} ^ {b} \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {1}} f ^ {\prime \prime} (s _ {2}) d s _ {2} d s _ {1}. \end{array}
$$

Continuing in this fashion, we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (b) = f (a) + f ^ {\prime} (a) (b - a) + f ^ {\prime \prime} (a) \int_ {a} ^ {b} \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {1}} \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {2}} d s _ {3} d s _ {2} d s _ {1} + \dots \\ \qquad + f ^ {(n - 1)} (a) \int_ {a} ^ {b} \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {1}} \dots \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {n - 1}} d s _ {n} \dots d s _ {1} \\ \qquad + \int_ {a} ^ {b} \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {1}} \dots \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {n - 1}} f ^ {(n)} (s _ {n}) d s _ {n} \dots d s _ {1}. \end{array}
$$

Now it is easy to prove by induction that 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {b} \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {1}} \dots \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {k - 1}} d s _ {k} \dots d s _ {1} = \frac {(b - a) ^ {k}}{k !}.\tag{1.3}
$$

Indeed, this is trivially true for $k = 1$ , and assuming that it holds for k, we have 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {b} \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {1}} \dots \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {k}} d s _ {k + 1} d s _ {k} \dots d s _ {1} = \int_ {a} ^ {b} \frac {(s _ {1} - a) ^ {k}}{k !} d s _ {1} = \frac {(b - a) ^ {k + 1}}{(k + 1) !},
$$

where the first equation follows from the induction hypothesis. 

As an easy corollary, we obtain Taylor’s formula in Lagrange’s form. 

## Corollary 1.4. Theorem 1.1 follows from Theorem 1.3.

Proof. By the mean value theorem there exists $\overline { { x } } \in \left( a , s _ { n - 1 } \right)$ such that 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {s _ {n - 1}} f ^ {(n)} (s _ {n}) d s _ {n} = f ^ {(n)} (\overline {{x}}) (s _ {n - 1} - a) = \int_ {a} ^ {s _ {n - 1}} f ^ {(n)} (\overline {{x}}) d s _ {n}.
$$

The proof is completed by substituting this in the iterated integral in the statement of Theorem 1.3 and using (1.3). □ 

Next, we give Taylor’s formula in Cauchy’s form. 

Theorem 1.5. Let f satisfy the conditions of Theorem 1.1. We have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (b) = f (a) + f ^ {\prime} (a) (b - a) + \frac {f ^ {\prime \prime} (a)}{2} (b - a) ^ {2} + \dots + \frac {f ^ {(n - 1)} (a)}{(n - 1) !} (b - a) ^ {n - 1} \\ \quad + \frac {1}{(n - 1) !} \int_ {a} ^ {b} f ^ {(n)} (x) (b - x) ^ {n - 1}   d x. \end{array}\tag{1.4}
$$

Proof. The domain of the iterated integral in the statement of Theorem 1.3 is $\left\{ \left( s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } \right) : a \leq s _ { n } \leq s _ { n - 1 } \leq \cdots \leq s _ { 1 } \leq b \right\}$ . By Fubini’s theorem, this integral can be written as 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {b} f ^ {(n)} (s _ {n}) \int_ {s _ {n}} ^ {b} \dots \int_ {s _ {2}} ^ {b} d s _ {1} \dots d s _ {n - 1} d s _ {n}.\tag{1.5}
$$

We claim that 

$$
\int_ {s _ {k}} ^ {b} \dots \int_ {s _ {2}} ^ {b} d s _ {1} \dots d s _ {k - 1} = \frac {(b - s _ {k}) ^ {k - 1}}{(k - 1) !}.
$$

Indeed, this is trivial to check for $k = 1$ . If it holds for k, then 

$$
\int_ {s _ {k + 1}} ^ {b} \dots \int_ {s _ {2}} ^ {b} d s _ {1} \dots d s _ {k} d s _ {k + 1} = \int_ {s _ {k + 1}} ^ {b} \frac {(b - s _ {k}) ^ {k - 1}}{(k - 1) !} d s _ {k} = \frac {(b - s _ {k + 1}) ^ {k}}{k !},
$$

where the first equality follows from the induction hypothesis. This proves the claim for $k + 1$ . Then the integral (1.5) becomes $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ^ { ( n ) } ( s _ { n } ) ( b - s _ { n } ) ^ { n - 1 } / ( n - 1 ) } \end{array}$ $1 ) ! d s _ { n }$ , and coincides with the one in (1.4). The theorem is proved. □ 

We now give a simple demonstration of the use of Taylor’s formula in optimization. Suppose that $x ^ { * }$ is a critical point, that is, $f ^ { \prime } ( x ^ { * } ) = 0$ . The quadratic Taylor’s formula gives 

$$
f (x) = f (x ^ {*}) + f ^ {\prime} (x ^ {*}) (x - x ^ {*}) + \frac {f ^ {\prime \prime} (\overline {{x}})}{2} (x - x ^ {*}) ^ {2},
$$

for some x strictly between x and $x ^ { * }$ . Now, if $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( { \overline { { x } } } ) \geq 0$ for all ${ \overline { { x } } } \in I$ , then 

$$
f (x) \geq f (x ^ {*}) \text {   for   all   } x \in I.
$$

This shows that $x ^ { * }$ is a global minimizer of f. A function f with $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x )$ nonnegative at all points is a convex function. If $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( { \overline { { x } } } ) \geq 0$ only in a neighborhood of $x ^ { * }$ , then $x ^ { * }$ is a local minimizer of f. If $f ^ { \prime } ( x ^ { * } ) = 0$ and $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) \leq 0$ for all $x ,$ then $f ( x ) \leq f ( x ^ { * } )$ , for all $x ,$ , that is, $x ^ { * }$ is a global maximizer of $f$ . Such a function f is a concave function. Chapter 4 treats convex and concave (not necessarily diferentiable) functions in detail. 

## 1.2 Diferentiation of Functions of Several Variables

Definition 1.6. Let $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ be a function on an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . If $x \in U$ , the limit 

$$
\frac {\partial f}{\partial x _ {i}} (x) := \lim _ {t \to 0} \frac {f (x _ {1} , \ldots , x _ {i - 1} , x _ {i} + t , x _ {i + 1} , \ldots , x _ {n}) - f (x)}{t},
$$

if it exists, is called the partial derivative of f at x with respect to $x _ { i }$ . If all the partial derivatives exist, then the vector 

$$
\nabla f (x) := (\partial f / \partial x _ {1}, \dots , \partial f / \partial x _ {n}) ^ {T}
$$

is called the gradient of f. 

Let $d \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ be a vector $d = ( d _ { 1 } , \ldots , d _ { n } ) ^ { T }$ . Denoting by $e _ { i }$ the ith coordinate vector 

$$
e _ {i} := (0, \dots , 1, 0, \dots , 0) ^ {T},
$$

where the only nonzero entry 1 is in the ith position, we have 

$$
d = d _ {1} e _ {1} + \dots + d _ {n} e _ {n}.
$$

Definition 1.7. The directional derivative of f at $x \in U$ along the direction $d \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ is 

$$
f ^ {\prime} (x; d) := \lim _ {t \searrow 0} \frac {f (x + t d) - f (x)}{t},
$$

provided the limit on the right-hand side exists as $t \geq 0$ approaches zero. 

Clearly, $f ^ { \prime } ( x ; \alpha d ) = \alpha f ^ { \prime } ( x ; d )$ for $\alpha \geq 0$ , and we note that if $f ^ { \prime } ( x ; - d ) =$ $- f ^ { \prime } ( x ; d )$ , then we have 

$$
f ^ {\prime} (x; d) = \lim _ {t \to 0} \frac {f (x + t d) - f (x)}{t},
$$

because 

$$
f ^ {\prime} (x; d) = - f ^ {\prime} (x, - d) = - \lim _ {t \searrow 0} \frac {f (x - t d) - f (x)}{t} = \lim _ {s \nearrow 0} \frac {f (x + s d) - f (x)}{s}.
$$

Definition 1.8. A function $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ is Gˆateaux diferentiable at $x \in U$ if the directional derivative $f ^ { \prime } ( x ; d )$ exists for all directions $d \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ and is a linear function of d. 

Let f be Gˆateaux diferentiable at x. Since $d = d _ { 1 } e _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + d _ { n } e _ { n }$ , and $f ^ { \prime } ( x ; d )$ is linear in d, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f ^ {\prime} (x; d) = f ^ {\prime} (x; d _ {1} e _ {1} + \dots + d _ {n} e _ {n}) = d _ {1} f ^ {\prime} (x; e _ {1}) + \dots + d _ {n} f ^ {\prime} (x; e _ {n}) \\ = \langle d, \nabla f (x) \rangle = d ^ {T} \nabla f (x). \end{array}
$$

Definition 1.9. The function $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ is Fr´echet diferentiable at the point $x \in U$ if there exists a linear function $\ell : \mathbb { R } ^ { n }  \mathbb { R } , \ell ( x ) = \langle l , x \rangle$ , such that 

$$
\lim _ {\| h \| \to 0} \frac {f (x + h) - f (x) - \langle l , h \rangle}{\| h \|} = 0.\tag{1.6}
$$

Intuitively speaking, this means that the function f can be “well approximated” around x by an afine function $h  f ( x ) + \langle l , h \rangle$ , that is, 

$$
f (x + h) \approx f (x) + \langle l, h \rangle .
$$

This approximate equation can be made precise using Landau’s little “oh” notation, where we call a vector $o ( h ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ if 

$$
\lim _ {h \to 0} \frac {\| o (h) \|}{\| h \|} = 0.
$$

With this notation, the Fr´echet diferentiability of $f$ at x is equivalent to stating $f ( x + h ) - f ( x ) - \langle l , h \rangle = o ( h )$ , or 

$$
f (x + h) = f (x) + \langle l, h \rangle + o (h).\tag{1.7}
$$

The $o ( h )$ notation is very intuitive and convenient to use in proofs involving limits. 

Clearly, if f is Fr´echet diferentiable at $x ,$ , then it is continuous at $x ,$ because (1.7) implies that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { h  0 } f ( x + h ) = f ( x ) } \end{array}$ 

The vector l in the definition of Fr´echet diferentiability can be calculated explicitly. Choosing $h = t e _ { i } \ ( i = 1 , \ldots , n )$ in (1.6) gives 

$$
\lim _ {t \to 0} \frac {f (x + t e _ {i}) - f (x) - t l _ {i}}{t} = 0.
$$

We have $l _ { i } = { \partial f ( x ) } / { \partial x _ { i } }$ , and thus 

$$
l = \nabla f (x).\tag{1.8}
$$

Then (1.7) becomes 

$$
f (x + h) = f (x) + \langle \nabla f (x), h \rangle + o (h).
$$

This also gives us the following Theorem. 

Theorem 1.10. If $U \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ is open and $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ is Fr´echet diferentiable at x, then f is Gˆateaux diferentiable at x. 

Thus, Fr´echet diferentiability implies Gˆateaux diferentiability, but the converse is not true; see the exercises at the end of the chapter. Consequently, Fr´echet diferentiability is a stronger concept than Gˆateaux diferentiability. In fact, the former concept is a uniform version of the latter: it is not hard to see that f is Fr´echet diferentiable at x if and only if f is Gˆateaux diferentiable and the limit 

$$
\lim _ {t \to 0} \frac {f (x + t d) - f (x) - \langle \nabla f (x) , d \rangle}{t}
$$

converges uniformly to zero for all $\| d \| \leq 1$ , that is, given $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
\left\| \frac {f (x + t d) - f (x) - \langle \nabla f (x) , d \rangle}{t} \right\| <   \varepsilon ,
$$

for all $| t | < \delta$ and for all $\| d \| \leq 1$ 

Definition 1.11. If x, y are two points in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , we denote by $[ x , y ]$ the closed line segment between x and y, that is, 

$$
[ x, y ] = \{x + t (y - x): 0 \leq t \leq 1 \}.
$$

Similarly, we use $( x , y )$ to denote the $\boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { \hat { \Pi } } } } ^ { o p e n } $ line segment $\{ x + t ( y - x ) : 0 <$ $t < 1 \}$ . Note that if $x = y$ , we have $[ x , y ] = ( x , y ) = \{ x \}$ 

Lemma 1.12. (Mean value theorem) Let $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ be a Gˆateaux differentiable function on an open set U in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . If x, y are distinct points in U such that the line segment $[ x , y ]$ lies in U, then there exists a point z on $( x , y )$ strictly between x and y, such that 

$$
f (y) = f (x) + \langle \nabla f (z), y - x \rangle .
$$

Proof. Define the function $h ( t ) = f ( x + t ( y - x ) )$ . Since f is Gˆateaux diferentiable, $h ( t )$ is diferentiable and 

$$
h ^ {\prime} (t) = \langle \nabla f (x + t (y - x)), y - x \rangle .
$$

It follows from the mean value theorem in one variable (Corollary 1.2) that there exists $0 < \bar { t } < 1$ such that $h ( 1 ) - h ( 0 ) = h ^ { \prime } ( \bar { t } )$ . Define $z = x + \bar { t } ( y - x )$ Since $h ( 0 ) = f ( x )$ and $h ( 1 ) = f ( y )$ , we see that 

$$
f (y) - f (x) = \langle \nabla f (z), y - x \rangle .
$$

Theorem 1.13. Let $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ be a function on an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . If $f ( x )$ is Gˆateaux diferentiable at $x _ { 0 } \in U$ and the partial derivatives $\partial f / \partial x _ { j }$ $( j = 1 , \ldots , n )$ are continuous at $x _ { 0 }$ , then f is Fr´echet diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ 

Proof. The mean value theorem (Lemma 1.12) implies that there exists a point x strictly between $x _ { 0 }$ and $x _ { 0 } + h$ such that 

$$
f (x _ {0} + h) - f (x _ {0}) - \langle \nabla f (x _ {0}), h \rangle = \langle \nabla f (\overline {{x}}) - \nabla f (x _ {0}), h \rangle ,
$$

and the continuity of $\nabla f$ at $x _ { 0 }$ implies that $\nabla f ( { \overline { { x } } } ) - \nabla f ( x _ { 0 } )  0$ as $h  0$ Therefore, 

$$
f (x _ {0} + h) - f (x _ {0}) - \langle \nabla f (x _ {0}), h \rangle = o (h),
$$

proving that f is Fr´echet diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ 

## 1.3 Diferentiability of Vector-Valued Functions

Let $F : U  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a function, where U is an open subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . We write 

$$
F (x) = F (x _ {1}, \ldots , x _ {n}) = \left( \begin{array}{c} f _ {1} (x) \\ f _ {2} (x) \\ \vdots \\ f _ {m} (x) \end{array} \right),
$$

where $f _ { i }$ is called the ith coordinate function of $F .$ 

Definition 1.14. The function F is called Gˆateaux diferentiable at $x \in U$ if 

$$
\lim _ {t \to 0} \frac {F (x + t d) - F (x)}{t}
$$

is linear in d, that is, there exists a linear map $T : \mathbb { R } ^ { n }  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , say $T ( x ) = A x$ , where A is an $m \times n$ matrix, such that 

$$
\lim _ {t \to 0} \frac {F (x + t d) - F (x)}{t} = A d.
$$

This equation means that 

$$
\lim _ {t \to 0} \frac {f _ {i} (x + t d) - f _ {i} (x)}{t} = \langle a ^ {i}, d \rangle ,
$$

where $a ^ { i }$ is the ith row of A. Thus, $F$ is Gˆateaux diferentiable if and only if each coordinate function $f _ { i }$ is. It follows from (1.8) that 

$$
a ^ {i} = \nabla f _ {i} (x) ^ {T} = (\partial f _ {i} / \partial x _ {1}, \ldots , \partial f _ {i} / \partial x _ {n}).
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c c} \partial f _ {1} / \partial x _ {1} & \ldots & \partial f _ {1} / \partial x _ {j} & \ldots & \partial f _ {1} / \partial x _ {n} \\ \vdots & & \vdots & & \vdots \\ \partial f _ {i} / \partial x _ {1} & \ldots & \partial f _ {i} / \partial x _ {j} & \ldots & \partial f _ {i} / \partial x _ {n} \\ \vdots & & \vdots & & \vdots \\ \partial f _ {m} / \partial x _ {1} & \ldots & \partial f _ {m} / \partial x _ {j} & \ldots & \partial f _ {m} / \partial x _ {n} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \nabla f _ {1} (x) ^ {T} \\ \vdots \\ \nabla f _ {m} (x) ^ {T} \end{array} \right] = [ \partial f _ {i} / \partial x _ {j} ].
$$

We denote A by $D F ( x )$ and call it the Jacobian of $F$ at x. Note that if $m = 1$ ， that is, $F$ is a scalar-valued function, then 

$$
D F (x) = \nabla F (x) ^ {T}.
$$

Definition 1.15. The function $F$ is called Fr´echet diferentiable at $x \in U$ if there exists a linear map $B : \mathbb { R } ^ { n }  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ satisfying 

$$
\lim _ {\| h \| \to 0} \frac {\| F (x + h) - F (x) - B h \|}{\| h \|} = 0.\tag{1.9}
$$

The map $B _ { z }$ , denoted by $D F ( x )$ , is called the Fr´echet derivative of $F$ . 

This equation means, as above, 

$$
\lim _ {\| h \| \to 0} \frac {| f _ {i} (x + h) - f _ {i} (x) - \langle b ^ {i} , h \rangle |}{\| h \|} = 0,
$$

for each $i ~ = ~ 1 , \ldots , m$ . In other words, $F$ is Fr´echet diferentiable at x if and only if each coordinate function $f _ { i }$ is. We have $b ^ { i } = \nabla f _ { i } ( x ) =$ $( \partial f _ { i } / \partial x _ { 1 } , \ldots , \partial f _ { i } / \partial x _ { n } ) ^ { T }$ , and 

$$
B = D F (x) = [ \partial f _ {i} (x) / \partial x _ {j} ].
$$

If $F$ is Fr´echet diferentiable at $x ,$ then $F$ is Gˆateaux diferentiable at x. Since $F$ is Fr´echet (Gˆateaux) diferentiable at x if and only if each coordinate function $f _ { i }$ is Fr´echet (Gˆateaux) diferentiable at $x ,$ this follows from previously proved results about scalar functions. 

## 1.4 The Chain Rule

Theorem 1.16. Let $F : U \to V , G : V \to \mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ , where $U \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ and $V \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ are open sets, and let $H = G \circ F : U  \mathbb { R } ^ { k } , H ( x ) = G ( F ( x ) ) = ( G \circ F ) ( x )$ be their composition. If F is Gˆateaux diferentiable at x and G is Fr´echet diferentiable at $y = F ( x )$ , then H is Gˆateaux diferentiable at x and 

$$
D H (x) = D G (y) \circ D F (x).
$$

Moreover, if F and G are Fr´echet diferentiable at x and $y = F ( x )$ , respectively, then H is Fr´echet diferentiable at x. 

Proof. Set $A = D F ( x )$ and $B = D G ( y )$ . We have 

$$
F (x + t d) = F (x) + t D F (x) d + o (t) = F (x) + t A d + o (t)
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & H (x + t d) = G (F (x + t d)) = G \big (F (x) + (t A d + o (t)) \big) \\ & \qquad = G (F (x)) + D G (F (x)) \big (t A d + o (t) \big) + o \big (t A d + o (t) \big) \\ & \qquad = H (x) + t B A d + B o (t) + o \big (t A d + o (t) \big) \\ & \qquad = H (x) + t B A d + o (t). \end{array}
$$

Comparing the above equation with 

$$
H (x + t d) = H (x) + t D H (x) d + o (t),
$$

we conclude that 

$$
D H (x) = B A = D G (y) \circ D F (x).
$$

This proves the first part of the theorem. 

If F is Fr´echet diferentiable at x, similar calculations show that 

$$
F (x + h) = F (x) + D F (x) h + o (h)
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} H (x + h) = G (F (x + h)) = G \left(F (x) + D F (x) h + o (h)\right) \\ = G (F (x)) + D G (F (x)) \left[ D F (x) h + o (h) \right] + o \left(D F (x) h + o (h)\right) \\ = H (x) + D G (F (x)) \circ D F (x) h + D G (F (x)) o (h) \\ \quad + o (D F (x) h + o (h)) \\ = H (x) + D G (y) \circ D F (x) h + o (h). \end{array}
$$

This shows that H is Fr´echet diferentiable. 

Exercise 16 on page 26 shows that the chain rule may fail under Gˆateaux diferentiability. 

The mean value theorem fails for vector-valued functions (see Exercise 13), but we have the following two very important substitutes. 

Lemma 1.17. Let $f : I  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a map on an interval $\boldsymbol { I } = \left( a , b \right)$ . If f is diferentiable at every point in I, then 

$$
\| f (y) - f (x) \| \leq | y - x | \cdot \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq 1} \| D f (x + t (y - x)) \|, \quad x, y \in I.
$$

Proof. Let $M > \operatorname* { s u p } _ { 0 \leq t \leq 1 } \| D f ( x + t ( y - x ) ) \|$ and set 

$$
K := \left\{t: 0 \leq t \leq 1, \| f (x + t (y - x)) - f (x) \| \leq M t | y - x | \right\}.
$$

The set $K$ is closed, since f is continuous, and $0 \in K$ . Let s be the largest element of K. We claim that $s = 1$ . Otherwise, $s < 1$ , and choosing $t \in ( s , 1 )$ such that $t - s$ is small enough, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \| f (x + t (y - x)) - f (x) \| \\ \leq & \| f (x + t (y - x)) - f (x + s (y - x)) \| + \| f (x + s (y - x)) - f (x) \| \\ \leq & \left\| D f (x + s (y - x)) (t - s) (y - x) + o ((t - s) | y - x |) \right\| + M s | y - x | \\ \leq & M (t - s) | y - x | + M s | y - x | \\ = & M t | y - x |, \end{array}
$$

that is, $t \in K$ , a contradiction. This proves the claim and the lemma. □ 

Theorem 1.18. Let $f : U \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be Gˆateaux diferentiable on an open set U in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n } . \mathrm { ~ } H \mathrm { ~ } x , y$ are points in U such that the line segment $[ x , y ]$ lies in $U$ , and $T : \mathbb { R } ^ { n }  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is a linear map, then 

$$
\| f (y) - f (x) - T (y - x) \| \leq \| y - x \| \cdot \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq 1} \| D f (x + t (y - x)) - T \|.
$$

Proof. The map $g ( t ) = f ( x + t ( y - x ) ) - t T ( y - x )$ is diferentiable with the derivative 

$$
D g (t) = [ D f (x + t (y - x)) - T ] (y - x).
$$

Lemma 1.17 gives $\| g ( 1 ) - g ( 0 ) \| \leq \operatorname* { s u p } _ { 0 \leq t \leq 1 } \| D g ( t ) \|$ , so that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \| f (y) - f (x) - T (y - x) \| \leq \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq 1} \| D f (x + t (y - x)) (y - x) - T (y - x) \| \\ \leq \| y - x \| \cdot \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq 1} \| D f (x + t (y - x)) - T \|. \end{array}
$$

Lemma 1.17 and Theorem 1.18 hold in a Banach space setting, with the same proof. 

Theorem 1.19. Let $F : U  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a map on an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . If $F ( x ) = ( f _ { 1 } ( x ) , \ldots , f _ { m } ( x ) ) ^ { T }$ is Gˆateaux diferentiable at $x _ { 0 } \in U$ and the partial derivatives ${ \partial f _ { i } } / { \partial x _ { j } } \ ( i = 1 , \ldots , m , j = 1 , \ldots , n )$ are continuous at $x _ { 0 }$ , then $F$ is Fr´echet diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ 

Proof. By Theorem 1.18, we have 

$$
\| f (x + h) - f (x) - D f (x) h \| \leq \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq 1} \| D f (x + t h) - D f (x) \| \cdot \| h \| = o (h)
$$

as $h \to 0$ , because $D f$ is continuous. 

□ 

Definition 1.20. Let $f : U \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a map on an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . We call f twice Fr´echet diferentiable on U if both f and Df are Fr´echet diferentiable on U, and denote by $D ^ { 2 } f : = D ( D f )$ the second derivative of f. By induction, we say that f is k-times Fr´echet diferentiable on U if f is $( k - 1 ) \cdot$ times Fr´echet diferentiable and $D ^ { k - 1 } f$ is Fr´echet diferentiable. We denote by $D ^ { k } f = D ( D ^ { k - 1 } f )$ the kth derivative of f. 

If $a \in U$ and u, $v \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , then we denote by $D ^ { 2 } f ( a ) [ u , v ]$ the directional derivative of the function $h ( x ) : = f ^ { \prime } ( x ; u )$ along direction v, that is, 

$$
D ^ {2} f (a) [ u, v ] := h ^ {\prime} (x; v).
$$

The operation of taking successive directional derivatives is commutative under suitable diferentiability assumptions. 

Theorem 1.21. If $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ is twice Fr´echet diferentiable on an open set U in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , then $D ^ { 2 } f ( a )$ is a symmetric bilinear form for all $a \in U$ , that is, 

$$
D ^ {2} f (a) [ u, v ] = D ^ {2} f (a) [ v, u ] \quad \text {   for   all   } \quad u, v \in \mathbb {R} ^ {n}.
$$

Proof. Define $g ( t ) : = f ( a + u + t v ) - f ( a + t v )$ . We have 

$$
g ^ {\prime} (t) = D f (a + u + t v) (v) - D f (a + t v) (v),
$$

and Lemma 1.17 applied to $g ( t ) - t g ^ { \prime } ( 0 )$ gives 

$$
\| g (1) - g (0) - g ^ {\prime} (0) \| \leq \sup _ {0 \leq t \leq 1} \| g ^ {\prime} (t) - g ^ {\prime} (0) \|.\tag{1.10}
$$

Since $D f$ is Fr´echet diferentiable, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} D f (a + u + t v) (v) - D f (a) (v) - D ^ {2} f (a) [ v, u + t v ] = o \big (\| v \| \cdot \| u + t v \| \big) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq o \big ((\| u \| + \| v \|) ^ {2} \big), \\ D f (a + t v) (v) - D f (a) (v) - D ^ {2} f (a) [ v, t v ] = o \big (\| v \| \cdot \| t v \| \big) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq o \big ((\| u \| + \| v \|) ^ {2} \big). \end{array}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first one gives 

$$
D f (a + u + t v) (v) - D f (a + t v) (v) - D ^ {2} f (a) [ v, u ] = o \big ((\| u \| + \| v \|) ^ {2} \big),
$$

that is, 

$$
g ^ {\prime} (t) - D ^ {2} f (a) [ v, u ] = o \big ((\| u \| + \| v \|) ^ {2} \big).
$$

Using this in (1.10) gives the equations $g ^ { \prime } ( t ) - g ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = o \big ( ( \lVert u \rVert + \lVert v \rVert ) ^ { 2 } \big )$ and 

$$
g (1) - g (0) - D ^ {2} f (a) [ v, u ] = o \big ((\| u \| + \| v \|) ^ {2} \big).
$$

Since $g ( 1 ) - g ( 0 ) = f ( a + u + v ) - f ( a + v ) - f ( a + u ) + f ( a )$ is symmetric in u and $v _ { : }$ , we similarly have 

$$
g (1) - g (0) - D ^ {2} f (a) [ u, v ] = o \big ((\| u \| + \| v \|) ^ {2} \big).
$$

Consequently, 

$$
B [ u, v ] := D ^ {2} f (a) [ u, v ] - D ^ {2} f (a) [ v, u ] = o ((\| u \| + \| v \|) ^ {2}).
$$

Let $\| u \| = \| v \| = 1$ , and let $t  0$ . We have $B [ t u , t v ] = o ( t ^ { 2 } )$ . Thus, $B [ u , v ] =$ $o ( t ^ { 2 } ) / t ^ { 2 } \to 0$ , that is, $B [ u , v ] = 0$ . This proves the symmetry of $D ^ { 2 } f ( a )$ □ 

Exercise 12 shows that $D ^ { 2 } f ( x ) [ u , v ] = D ^ { 2 } f ( x ) [ v , u ]$ may fail in the absence of suficient diferentiability assumptions. 

Corollary 1.22. If $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ is k-times Fr´echet diferentiable on an open set $U$ in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ and $a \in U$ , then $D ^ { k } f ( a )$ is a symmetric k-linear form, that is, 

$$
D ^ {k} f (a) \left[ u _ {\sigma (1)}, \dots , u _ {\sigma (k)} \right] = D ^ {k} f (a) \left[ u _ {1}, \dots , u _ {k} \right] \text {   for   all   } u _ {1}, \dots , u _ {k} \in E,
$$

where $\sigma$ is a permutation of the set $\{ 1 , 2 , \ldots , k \}$ 

The proof is obtained from Theorem 1.21 by induction. 

## 1.5 Taylor’s Formula for Functions of Several Variables

Taylor’s formula for a function of a single variable extends to a function $f$ : $U \to \mathbb { R }$ defined on an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . For this purpose, we restrict $f$ to line segments in $U$ . Let $\{ x + t d : t \in \mathbb { R } \}$ be a line passing through x and having the direction $d \neq 0 \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . Define the function $h ( t ) = f ( g ( t ) ) = f ( x + t d ) =$ $( f \circ g ) ( t )$ , where $g ( t ) = x + t d$ . It follows from the chain rule that 

$$
h ^ {\prime} (t) = \langle \nabla f (x + t d), d \rangle = \frac {\partial f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {1}} d _ {1} + \dots + \frac {\partial f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {n}} d _ {n}.
$$

Diferentiating $h ^ { \prime }$ using the chain rule again, we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} h ^ {\prime \prime} (t) = \left\langle \nabla (\frac {\partial f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {1}}), d \right\rangle d _ {1} + \dots + \left\langle \nabla (\frac {\partial f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {n}}), d \right\rangle d _ {n} \\ \quad = \left(\frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {1}} (\frac {\partial f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {1}}) d _ {1} + \dots + \frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {n}} (\frac {\partial f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {1}}) d _ {n}\right) d _ {1} + \dots \\ \quad \quad + \left(\frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {1}} (\frac {\partial f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {n}}) d _ {1} + \dots + \frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {n}} (\frac {\partial f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {n}}) d _ {n}\right) d _ {n} \\ \quad = \left(\frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {1} ^ {2}} d _ {1} ^ {2} + \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {2} \partial x _ {1}} d _ {2} d _ {1} + \dots + \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {n} \partial x _ {1}} d _ {n} d _ {1}\right) \\ \quad \quad + \dots + \left(\frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {1} \partial x _ {n}} d _ {1} d _ {n} + \dots + \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {n} ^ {2}} d _ {n} ^ {2}\right) \\ \quad = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {i} \partial x _ {j}} d _ {i} d _ {j}. \end{array}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} h ^ {\prime \prime} (t) = (d _ {1}, \ldots , d _ {n}) \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {1} ^ {2}} & \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {j} \partial x _ {1}} & \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {n} \partial x _ {1}} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {1} \partial x _ {i}} & \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {j} \partial x _ {i}} & \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {n} \partial x _ {i}} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {1} \partial x _ {n}} & \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {j} \partial x _ {n}} & \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {n} ^ {2}} \end{array} \right] \left( \begin{array}{c} d _ {1} \\ \vdots \\ d _ {n} \end{array} \right) \\ = d ^ {T} \left[ \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {j} \partial x _ {i}} \right] d = d ^ {T} D ^ {2} f (x + t d) d. \end{array}
$$

The matrix 

$$
H f (x) := D ^ {2} F (x) = D (\nabla f (x)) = [ \partial^ {2} f (x) / \partial x _ {i} \partial x _ {j} ]
$$

is called the Hessian matrix of $f$ at x. If the second-order partial derivatives $\partial ^ { 2 } f ( x ) / \partial x _ { i } \partial x _ { j }$ are continuous, then the mixed derivatives are equal, that is, 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {2} f (x)}{\partial x _ {i} \partial x _ {j}} = \frac {\partial^ {2} f (x)}{\partial x _ {j} \partial x _ {i}},
$$

and the Hessian matrix $H f ( x )$ is symmetric, that is, $H f ( x ) ^ { T } = H f ( x )$ 

One can keep diferentiating $h ( t )$ to obtain 

$$
h ^ {(3)} (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\partial^ {3} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {i} \partial x _ {j} \partial x _ {k}} d _ {i} d _ {j} d _ {k} = D ^ {3} f (x + t d) [ d, d, d ],
$$

and in general 

$$
h ^ {(k)} (t) = \sum_ {i _ {1} = 1} ^ {n} \dots \sum_ {i _ {k} = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\partial^ {k} f (x + t d)}{\partial x _ {i _ {1}} \cdots \partial x _ {i _ {k}}} d _ {i _ {1}} d _ {i _ {2}} \dots d _ {i _ {k}} = D ^ {k} f (x + t d) \underbrace {[ d , \ldots , d ]} _ {k \text { times}}.
$$

We note that $A [ d , \dotsc , d ] = D ^ { k } f ( x ) [ d , \dotsc , d ]$ is a k-linear form, which gives rise to a k-linear functional $A [ d _ { 1 } , \ldots , d _ { k } ]$ . If the kth-order partial derivatives are continuous, then $A [ d _ { 1 } , \ldots , d _ { k } ]$ is symmetric, that is, 

$$
A [ d _ {\sigma (1)}, \dots , d _ {\sigma (k)} ] = A [ d _ {1}, \dots , d _ {k} ],
$$

for any permutation $\sigma$ of the set $\{ 1 , \ldots , k \}$ 

After these preparations, we can display the multivariate Taylor’s formula. 

Theorem 1.23. (Multivariate Taylor’s formula) Let U be an open subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , and let x, y be distinct points in U such that the line segment $[ x , y ]$ lies in U. If $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ has continuous kth-order partial derivatives on U, then there exists a point $z \in ( x , y )$ such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (y) = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {k - 1} \frac {1}{i !} D ^ {i} f (x) \big [ \underbrace {y - x , \ldots , y - x} _ {i \text { times}} \big ] + \frac {1}{k !} D ^ {k} f (z) \big [ \underbrace {y - x , \ldots , y - x} _ {k + 1 \text { times }} \big ] \\ = f (x) + D f (x) [ y - x ] + \frac {1}{2} D ^ {2} f (x) [ y - x, y - x ] + \dots \\ \quad + \frac {1}{(k - 1) !} D ^ {k - 1} f (x) [ y - x, \ldots , y - x ] + \frac {1}{k !} D ^ {k} f (z) [ y - x, \ldots , y - x ]. \end{array}
$$

Here 

$$
\begin{array}{c} {D f (x) [ y - x ] = \langle \nabla f (x), y - x \rangle ,} \\ {D ^ {2} f (x) [ y - x, y - x ] = (y - x) ^ {T} H f (x) (y - x) = d ^ {T} H (x) d.} \end{array}
$$

Proof. It follows from Taylor’s formula for h that there exists $0 < \bar { t } < 1$ such that 

$$
h (1) = h (0) + h ^ {\prime} (0) + \frac {h ^ {\prime \prime} (0)}{2 !} + \dots + \frac {h ^ {(k - 1)} (0)}{(k - 1) !} + \frac {h ^ {(k)} (\bar {t})}{k !}.
$$

We note that $h ( 1 ) = f ( y ) , h ( 0 ) = f ( x ) , h ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = \langle \nabla f ( x ) , y - x \rangle$ , and $h ^ { \prime \prime } ( 0 ) =$ $D ^ { 2 } f ( x ) [ d , d ] = d ^ { T } H ( x ) d .$ . In general, 

$$
h ^ {(i)} (t) = D ^ {i} f (x + t (y - x)) [ y - x, \ldots , y - x ].
$$

Setting $z = x + { \bar { t } } ( y - x )$ , we see that the Taylor’s formula in the statement of the theorem holds. □ 

Corollary 1.24. Let U be an open subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , and let $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ have continuous kth-order partial derivatives on U. Then, as y approaches x, 

$$
f (y) = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {k} \frac {1}{i !} D ^ {i} f (x) \big [ \underbrace {y - x , \ldots , y - x} _ {i \text { times }} \big ] + o (\| y - x \| ^ {k}).
$$

We remark that in light of Exercise 1, the corollary holds under the weaker assumption that f is k-times Fr´echet diferentiable. 

Usually, Taylor’s formula is considered for $k = 1 , 2 , 3$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (y) = f (x) + \langle \nabla f (z _ {1}), y - x \rangle , \\ f (y) = f (x) + \langle \nabla f (x), y - x \rangle + \frac {1}{2} (y - x) ^ {T} H f (z _ {2}) (y - x), \\ f (y) = f (x) + \langle \nabla f (x), y - x \rangle + \frac {1}{2} (y - x) ^ {T} H f (x) (y - x) \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{6} D ^ {3} f (z _ {3}) [ y - x, y - x, y - x ], \end{array}
$$

where $z _ { i } \in ( x , y ) , i = 1 , 2 , 3 . \mathrm { A s } y \to x$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & f (y) = f (x) + \langle \nabla f (x), y - x \rangle + o (\| y - x \|), \\ & f (y) = f (x) + \langle \nabla f (x), y - x \rangle + \frac {1}{2} (y - x) ^ {T} H f (x) (y - x) + o (\| y - x \| ^ {2}), \\ & f (y) = f (x) + \langle \nabla f (x), y - x \rangle + \frac {1}{2} (y - x) ^ {T} H f (x) (y - x) \\ & \qquad + \frac {1}{6} D ^ {3} f (x) [ y - x, y - x, y - x ] + o (\| y - x \| ^ {3}). \end{array}
$$

## 1.6 The Converse of Taylor’s Theorem

Taylor’s theorem has the following converse. 

Theorem 1.25. Let U be an open subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . If a continuous function $f : U \to \mathbb { R }$ satisfies 

$$
f (x + y) = a _ {0} (x) + a _ {1} (x) [ y ] + \frac {1}{2} a _ {2} (x) [ y ^ {2} ] + \dots + \frac {1}{k !} a _ {k} (x) [ y ^ {k} ] + o (\| y \| ^ {k}),\tag{1.11}
$$

where $a _ { i } ( x )$ is a symmetric i-linear form on $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ and where we have written $a _ { k } [ y ^ { k } ]$ for $a _ { k } ( x ) [ y , \dots , y ]$ to simplify notation, then f is k-times Fr´echet differentiable and $a _ { i } ( x ) = D ^ { i } f ( x ) , i = 1 , \dots , k$ 

Proof. We use induction on k. For $k = 0 , 1$ , the theorem is true by the continuity of f and the definition of Fr´echet diferentiability, respectively. Suppose the theorem is true for $k - 1$ . Then, $a _ { k } ( x ) [ y ^ { k } ] = o ( \| y \| ^ { k - 1 } )$ in (1.11), and the induction hypothesis implies that $a _ { j } ( x ) = D ^ { j } f ( x )$ for $j = 0 , \ldots , k - 1$ . We now expand $f ( x + y + z )$ in two ways, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f (x + y + z) = f (x + y) + D f (x + y) [ z ] + \dots + \frac {D ^ {k - 1} f (x + y) [ z ^ {k - 1} ]}{(k - 1) !} \\ + \frac {1}{k !} a _ {k} (x + y) [ z ^ {k} ] + o (\| y \| ^ {k}) \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f (x + y + z) = f (x) + D f (x) [ y + z ] + \dots + \frac {D ^ {k - 1} f (x) [ (y + z) ^ {k - 1} ]}{(k - 1) !} \\ + \frac {1}{k !} a _ {k} (x) [ (y + z) ^ {k} ] + o (\| y + z \| ^ {k}). \end{array}
$$

Fix x, and restrict z such that the ratio $\| y \| / 2 \le \| z \| \le \| y \|$ . Then $o ( \| z \| ^ { i } )$ 1 $o ( \| y \| ^ { i } )$ , and $o ( \| y + z \| ^ { i } )$ are all equivalent. Subtracting the second equation above from the first one, collecting coeficients of $[ z ^ { i } ]$ , and denoting by $g _ { i } ( y )$ the coeficient of $[ z ^ { i } ]$ , we have 

$$
g _ {0} (y) + g _ {1} (y) [ z ] + \dots + g _ {k} (y) [ z ^ {k} ] = o (\| y \| ^ {k}).\tag{1.12}
$$

Note that 

$$
g _ {k} (y) [ z ^ {k} ] = \frac {1}{k !} \left(a _ {k} (x + y) - a _ {k} (x)\right) [ z ^ {k} ] = o (\| y \| ^ {k}),
$$

since $\begin{array} { r } { a _ { k } ( x + y ) - a _ { k } ( x ) = o ( 1 ) } \end{array}$ by the continuity of $a _ { k }$ . Thus, this term may be dropped from equation (1.12). We claim that each remaining term in (1.12) is also $o ( \| y \| ^ { k } )$ . To prove this, we replace z with $t _ { i } z$ , where $\{ t _ { i } \} _ { 1 } ^ { k }$ are all distinct. Then the resulting equations may be written as 

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c c c c} 1 & t _ {1} & \dots & t _ {1} ^ {k} \\ 1 & t _ {2} & \dots & t _ {2} ^ {k} \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 1 & t _ {k} & \dots & t _ {k} ^ {k} \end{array} \right] \left( \begin{array}{c} g _ {0} (y) \\ g _ {1} (y) [ z ] \\ \vdots \\ g _ {k - 1} (y) [ z ^ {k - 1} ] \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} o (\| y \| ^ {k}) \\ o (\| y \| ^ {k}) \\ \vdots \\ o (\| y \| ^ {k}) \end{array} \right).
$$

Since $t _ { i }$ are distinct, the Vandermonde matrix above has determinant $\Pi _ { i < j } ( t _ { i } -$ $t _ { j } ) \neq 0$ , so that it is nonsingular. It follows by Cramer’s rule that $g _ { i } ( y ) [ z ^ { i } ] =$ $o ( \| y \| ^ { k } )$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , k - 1$ . In particular, 

$$
g _ {k - 1} (y) \left[ z ^ {k - 1} \right] = \left[ \frac {D ^ {k - 1} f (x + y)}{(k - 1) !} - \frac {D ^ {k - 1} f (x)}{(k - 1) !} - \frac {k a _ {k} (x) [ y ]}{k !} \right] \left[ z ^ {k - 1} \right] = o \left(\| y \| ^ {k}\right),
$$

where the expression involving $a _ { k } ( x )$ follows since the symmetry of $a _ { k } ( y )$ gives $a _ { k } ( y ) [ ( y + z ) ^ { k } ] = k a _ { k } ( y ) [ y , z , z , \dots , z ] + \cdot \cdot \cdot$ . This gives 

$$
D ^ {k - 1} f (x + y) - D ^ {k - 1} f (x) - a _ {k} (x) [ y ] = o (\| y \|),
$$

which implies $a _ { k } ( x ) = D ^ { k } f ( x )$ 

The simple proof above is in [203]. See also [3] for a more general form of this theorem. 

The significance of Theorem 1.25 is that Taylor’s formula is often a very eficient tool for computing the derivatives $D ^ { k } f ( x )$ of a multivariate function. 

If we can develop the function $t \mapsto f ( x + t d )$ as a series in t in some way, then the coeficient of $t ^ { k }$ is $D ^ { k } f ( x ) [ d , \dots , d ] / k !$ by Theorem 1.25, and we can recover $D ^ { k } f$ easily. 

We illustrate this technique with some important examples. 

Example 1.26. (Quadratic functions) Let 

$$
f (x) = \frac {1}{2} \langle A x, x \rangle + \langle c, x \rangle + \alpha = \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} a _ {i j} x _ {i} x _ {j} + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} c _ {j} x _ {j} + \alpha
$$

be a quadratic function in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , where A is a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix, $c \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , and α is a scalar. It is easy but tedious to compute the gradient and Hessian of f by computing the first-order and second-order partial derivatives of $f .$ 

Alternatively, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & f (x + t d) = \frac {1}{2} \langle A (x + t d), x + t d \rangle + \langle c, x + t d \rangle + \alpha \\ & \qquad = \frac {1}{2} \langle A x, x \rangle + t \langle A x, d \rangle + \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \langle A d, d \rangle + \langle c, x \rangle + t \langle c, d \rangle + \alpha \\ & \qquad = f (x) + t \langle A x + c, d \rangle + \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \langle A d, d \rangle . \end{array}
$$

Theorem 1.25 implies that 

$$
\nabla f (x) = A x + c, \quad H f (x) = D ^ {2} f (x) = A.
$$

These formulas apply without change to any quadratic function in an inner product space E if A is a self-adjoint (symmetric) linear operator $A : E  E$ 

## Example 1.27. (Logarithm of the determinant function)

Let us first consider the vector space $R ^ { n \times n }$ of $n \times n$ matrices. This is a vector space of dimension $n ^ { 2 }$ . A natural inner product on $\mathbb { R } ^ { n \times n }$ is given by 

$$
\langle X, Y \rangle := \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {n} x _ {i j} y _ {i j} = \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {n} (X ^ {T}) _ {j i} y _ {i j} = \operatorname{tr} (X ^ {T} Y).
$$

Next, we consider the linear subspace $S ^ { n }$ of symmetric $n \times n$ matrices of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n \times n }$ This is a vector space of dimension $n ( n + 1 ) / 2$ . The trace inner product on $\mathbb { R } ^ { n \times n }$ induces an inner product on $S ^ { n }$ given by 

$$
\langle X, Y \rangle := \operatorname{tr} (X Y).
$$

Let us now consider the function 

$$
f (X) = \ln \det X,
$$

where $X \in S ^ { n }$ is positive definite, an important function in semidefinite programming. 

We compute the Taylor series of f at a given positive definite matrix $X \in S ^ { n }$ and a given direction $D \in S ^ { n }$ . We have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f (X + t D) = \ln \det (X + t D) = \ln \det (X ^ {1 / 2} (I + t X ^ {- 1 / 2} D X ^ {- 1 / 2}) X ^ {1 / 2}) \\ = \ln \det X + \ln \det (I + t X ^ {- 1 / 2} D X ^ {- 1 / 2}). \end{array}
$$

Writing $\overline { { D } } : = X ^ { - 1 / 2 } D X ^ { - 1 / 2 } = Q ^ { T } A Q$ , where $Q$ is an orthogonal matrix and $\varLambda = \mathrm { d i a g } ( \lambda _ { 1 } , \ldots , \lambda _ { n } )$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f (X + t D) - f (X) = \ln \det (I + t \overline {{D}}) = \ln \det (Q ^ {T} (I + t \Lambda) Q) \\ = \ln \det (I + t \Lambda) = \ln \prod_ {i} ^ {n} (1 + t \lambda_ {i}) = \sum_ {1} ^ {n} \ln (1 + t \lambda_ {i}). \end{array}
$$

Since 

$$
\ln (1 + s) = \int {\frac {d s}{1 + s}} = \int (1 - s + s ^ {2} - s ^ {3} + \dots) d s = s - \frac {s ^ {2}}{2} + \frac {s ^ {3}}{3} + \dots ,
$$

we have 

$$
f (X + t D) - f (X) = \sum_ {1} ^ {n} t \lambda_ {i} - \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \lambda_ {i} ^ {2} + o (t ^ {2}) = t \operatorname{tr} (\Lambda) - \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \operatorname{tr} (\Lambda^ {2}) + o (t ^ {2}).
$$

Noting that 

$$
\operatorname{tr} (\Lambda) = \operatorname{tr} (Q ^ {T} \Lambda Q) = \operatorname{tr} (\overline {{D}}) = \operatorname{tr} (X ^ {- 1} D) = \langle X ^ {- 1}, D \rangle ,
$$

and similarly 

$$
\operatorname{tr} \left(\Lambda^ {2}\right) = \operatorname{tr} \left(X ^ {- 1 / 2} D X D ^ {- 1 / 2}\right) ^ {2} = \operatorname{tr} \left(X ^ {- 1} D X ^ {- 1} D\right) = \langle X ^ {- 1} D X ^ {- 1}, D \rangle ,
$$

we obtain 

$$
f (X + t D) = f (X) + t \langle X ^ {- 1}, D \rangle - \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \langle X ^ {- 1} D X ^ {- 1}, D \rangle + o (t ^ {2}).
$$

Theorem 1.25 again implies that $\nabla f ( X ) = X ^ { - 1 }$ and $D ^ { 2 } f ( X ) ( D ) = X ^ { - 1 } D X ^ { - 1 }$ Here $D ^ { 2 } f ( X ) ( D )$ can be written, using the tensor (Kronecker) product notation, 

$$
(X ^ {- 1} \otimes X ^ {- 1}) (D) := X ^ {- 1} D X ^ {- 1}.
$$

In summary, we have 

$$
\nabla f (X) = X ^ {- 1}, \quad D ^ {2} f (X) = - X ^ {- 1} \otimes X ^ {- 1}.\tag{1.13}
$$

Higher-order derivatives of $f$ can be obtained by computing more terms in the Taylor expansion above. 

The derivative of the determinant of not necessarily symmetric matrices is considered in Exercise 22 at the end of the chapter. See also Exercise 23. 

## Example 1.28. (Matrix inversion)

Denote by $\operatorname { G L } ( n , \mathbb { R } )$ the set of nonsingular matrices in the vector space $V = R ^ { n \times n }$ of $n \times n$ real matrices. We will show that the matrix inversion map 

$$
\operatorname{Inv}: \mathrm{GL} (n, \mathbb {R}) \to \mathrm{GL} (n, \mathbb {R}), \quad \operatorname{Inv} (A) = A ^ {- 1}
$$

is infinitely diferentiable, and compute its derivatives. 

First, we have from $( I + A ) ( I - A + A ^ { 2 } - A ^ { 3 } + ( - 1 ) ^ { k } A ^ { k } ) = I - A ^ { k + 1 } .$ Neumann’s formula 

$$
(I + A) ^ {- 1} = I - A + A ^ {2} - A ^ {3} + \dots \text { for } \| A \| <   1.
$$

It follows that for t small, 

$$
(I + t A) ^ {- 1} = I - t A + t ^ {2} A ^ {2} - t ^ {3} A ^ {3} + \dots = \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} (- 1) ^ {k} t ^ {k} A ^ {k},
$$

which immediately gives that 

$$
D ^ {k} \operatorname{Inv} (I) [ A, \dots , A ] = (- 1) ^ {k} k! A ^ {k}.
$$

Now, if $A \in \operatorname { G L } ( n , \mathbb { R } )$ and $H \in V$ are arbitrary matrices, and $K : = A ^ { - 1 } H$ we have 

$$
(A + t H) ^ {- 1} = [ A (I + A ^ {- 1} H) ] ^ {- 1} = (I + t K) ^ {- 1} A ^ {- 1} = \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} (- 1) ^ {k} t ^ {k} K ^ {k} A ^ {- 1},
$$

and we obtain 

$$
D ^ {k} \operatorname{Inv} (A) [ H, \dots , H ] = (- 1) ^ {k} k! A ^ {- 1} H A ^ {- 1} H \dots A ^ {- 1} H A ^ {- 1},
$$

where the right-hand side contains $k + 1 \ A ^ { \prime } \mathrm { s }$ and k H’s. 

These results extend verbatim to inversion of nonsingular continuous linear mappings $A : X \to X$ where X is a Banach space. 

## 1.7 Danskin’s Theorem

Danskin’s theorem [65, 66] is one of the fundamental theorems in optimization theory. We will use it in Chapters 9 and 12 to derive optimality conditions for nonlinear programming and semi-infinite programming, respectively. 

Theorem 1.29. (Danskin) Suppose $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb { R }$ is a continuous function, where $X \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ is an open set, Y is a compact set of a topological space $F _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , and $\nabla _ { x } f ( x , y )$ exists and is continuous. Then the marginal function 

$$
\varphi (x) := \max _ {y \in Y} f (x, y)
$$

is continuous and has directional derivatives in every direction, which are given by the formula 

$$
\varphi^ {\prime} (x; h) = \max _ {y \in Y (x)} \langle \nabla_ {x} f (x, y), h \rangle ,\tag{1.14}
$$

where $Y ( x ) = \{ y \in Y : \varphi ( x ) = f ( x , y ) \}$ is the set of maximizers in the definition $o f \varphi ( x )$ 

Proof. We first prove that $\varphi ( x )$ is continuous. Let $x _ { 0 } \in X$ and let $\{ x _ { k } \} _ { 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be a sequence converging to $x _ { 0 }$ . Pick $y _ { k } \in Y$ such that $\varphi ( x _ { k } ) = f ( x _ { k } , y _ { k } )$ . Since Y is compact, we may assume without loss of generality that $y _ { k } \to y _ { 0 } \in Y$ Noting that $f ( x _ { k } , y _ { k } ) \ge f ( x _ { k } , y )$ for any $y \in Y$ , we have 

$$
\lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} \varphi (x _ {k}) = \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} f (x _ {k}, y _ {k}) = f (x _ {0}, y _ {0}) \geq \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} f (x _ {k}, y) = f (x _ {0}, y),
$$

for all $y \in Y$ . The inequality $f ( x _ { 0 } , y _ { 0 } ) \ge f ( x _ { 0 } , y )$ implies $\varphi ( x _ { 0 } ) = f ( x _ { 0 } , y _ { 0 } )$ and we have $\begin{array} { r } { \varphi ( x _ { 0 } ) = f ( x _ { 0 } , y _ { 0 } ) = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { k \to \infty } \varphi ( x _ { k } ) } \end{array}$ , that is, $\varphi ( x )$ is continuous. 

Let $0 \neq h \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ be a direction, and let $\{ x _ { k } \} _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } , x _ { k } = x _ { 0 } + t _ { k } h , t _ { k } \geq 0 ,$ be a sequence converging to $x _ { 0 }$ . Let $y ~ \in ~ Y ( x _ { 0 } )$ be an arbitrary point. If $\varphi ( x _ { k } ) = f ( x _ { k } , y _ { k } ) ( k \geq 1 )$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\varphi (x _ {k}) - \varphi (x _ {0})}{t _ {k}} = \frac {f (x _ {k} , y _ {k}) - f (x _ {0} , y)}{t _ {k}} \\ \qquad = \frac {f (x _ {k} , y _ {k}) - f (x _ {k} , y)}{t _ {k}} + \frac {f (x _ {k} , y) - f (x _ {0} , y)}{t _ {k}} \\ \qquad \geq \frac {f (x _ {k} , y) - f (x _ {0} , y)}{t _ {k}} \\ \qquad = \langle \nabla_ {x} f (x _ {0} + t _ {k} ^ {\prime} h, y), h \rangle , \end{array}
$$

where the inequality follows since $f ( x _ { k } , y _ { k } ) \ge f ( x _ { k } , y )$ , and the last equality follows from the mean value theorem. Taking limits, we obtain 

$$
\varliminf_ {k \to \infty} \frac {\varphi (x _ {k}) - \varphi (x _ {0})}{t _ {k}} \geq \langle \nabla_ {x} f (x _ {0}, y), h \rangle \text {   for   all   } y \in Y (x _ {0}).
$$

This implies 

$$
\varliminf_ {k \to \infty} \frac {\varphi (x _ {k}) - \varphi (x _ {0})}{t _ {k}} \geq \max _ {y \in Y (x _ {0})} \langle \nabla_ {x} f (x _ {0}, y), h \rangle .\tag{1.15}
$$

Similarly, if $\varphi ( x _ { k } ) = f ( x _ { k } , y _ { k } ) ( k \geq 0 )$ , where $y _ { k }  y _ { 0 }$ , we also have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \frac {\varphi (x _ {k}) - \varphi (x _ {0})}{t _ {k}} & = \frac {f (x _ {k} , y _ {k}) - f (x _ {0} , y _ {k})}{t _ {k}} + \frac {f (x _ {0} , y _ {k}) - f (x _ {0} , y _ {0})}{t _ {k}} \\ & \leq \frac {f (x _ {k} , y _ {k}) - f (x _ {0} , y _ {k})}{t _ {k}} \\ & = \langle \nabla_ {x} f (x _ {0} + t _ {k} ^ {\prime \prime} h, y _ {k}), h \rangle . \end{array}
$$

This implies that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \varlimsup_ {k \to \infty} \frac {\varphi (x _ {k}) - \varphi (x _ {0})}{t _ {k}} \leq \varlimsup_ {i \to \infty} \langle \nabla_ {x} f (x _ {0} + t _ {k _ {i}} ^ {\prime} h, y _ {k _ {i}}), h \rangle \\ = \langle \nabla_ {x} f (x _ {0}, y _ {0}), h \rangle \\ \leq \max _ {y \in Y (x _ {0})} \langle \nabla_ {x} f (x _ {0}, y), h \rangle . \end{array}
$$

This inequality and (1.15) prove (1.14). 

We remark that Danskin’s theorem and its proof above hold verbatim if X is an open set in a Banach space. It can also be generalized in other ways; for example, in the case where Y is a finite set, the directional diferentiability of $x \mapsto f ( x , y )$ for each $y$ is enough to guarantee the directional diferentiability of $\varphi$ . 

Corollary 1.30. Let $\{ f _ { i } \} _ { 1 } ^ { k }$ be functions defined on a set X in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , and let $\varphi ( x ) : = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ f _ { i } ( x ) : i = 1 , \ldots , k \}$ be their pointwise maximum. $I f$ all $f _ { i }$ are directionally diferentiable at x in the direction $h \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , then $\varphi$ is directionally diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ in the direction $h _ { : }$ , and 

$$
\varphi^ {\prime} (x; h) = \max _ {y \in I} f _ {i} ^ {\prime} (x; h),
$$

where $I = \{ i : \varphi ( x ) = f _ { i } ( x ) \}$ 

This can be proved by mimicking the proof of Theorem 1.29. We leave it to the reader; see Exercise 24. 

## 1.8 Exercises

1. Let $f : I = ( c , d ) \to \mathbb { R }$ be an n-times diferentiable function. Show that 

$$
f (x) = f (a) + f ^ {\prime} (a) (x - a) + \dots + \frac {f ^ {(n)} (a)}{n !} (x - a) ^ {n} + o ((x - a) ^ {n}).
$$

The point of the exercise is to prove the above equality without assuming that f n-times continuously diferentiable, because if $f ^ { ( n ) }$ is continuous, then the equality follows readily from Theorem 1.1. 

Hint: Prove the equality 

$$
\lim _ {x \to a} \frac {f (x) - f (a) - f ^ {\prime} (a) (x - a) - \cdots - \frac {f ^ {(n)} (a)}{n !} (x - a) ^ {n}}{(x - a) ^ {n}} = 0,
$$

using induction on n, passing from n to $n + 1$ using L’Hospital’s rule. 

2. This exercise gives a fairly simple approach to Taylor’s formula in Cauchy’s form (Theorem 1.5) using integration by parts. The idea is to write 

$$
f (b) - f (a) = \int_ {a} ^ {b} f ^ {\prime} (x) d x = - \int_ {a} ^ {b} f ^ {\prime} (x) d (b - x),
$$

and then use integration by parts on the last integral. This gives 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f (b) = f (a) - f ^ {\prime} (x) (b - x) | _ {a} ^ {b} + \int_ {a} ^ {b} (b - x) f ^ {\prime \prime} (x) d x \\ = f (a) + f ^ {\prime} (a) (b - a) + \int_ {a} ^ {b} (b - x) f ^ {\prime \prime} (x) d x, \end{array}
$$

which is Theorem 1.5 for $n = 2$ 

(a) Use integration by parts on the last integral above to prove the theorem for $n = 3$ 

(b) Use induction on n to complete the proof of Theorem 1.5. 

3. This exercise outlines an interesting approach to Taylor’s formula in Cauchy’s form. 

Let $f : J  \mathbb { R }$ be a function on an open interval J, diferentiable enough times. Consider the operations 

$$
A: f (x) \mapsto \int_ {a} ^ {x} f (t) d t, \quad B: f (x) \mapsto f ^ {\prime} (x), \quad I: f (x) \mapsto f (x).
$$

Show that $B A ( f ( x ) ) ~ = ~ f ( x )$ , but $A B ( f ( x ) ) \ = \ f ( x ) - f ( a )$ , so that $A B \ne B A$ , that is, A and B do not commute, when $f ( a ) \neq 0$ . Obviously, $B ^ { k } ( f ( x ) ) = f ^ { ( k ) } ( x )$ . The formula for $A ^ { k }$ is more complicated. Show that 

$$
A ^ {2} (f (x)) = \int_ {a} ^ {x} \int_ {a} ^ {s} f (t) d t d s = \int_ {a} ^ {x} \int_ {t} ^ {x} f (t) d s d t = \int_ {a} ^ {x} (x - t) f (t) d t,
$$

where the second equality follows from Fubini’s theorem for multiple in tegrals. More generally, show that 

$$
A ^ {k} (f (x)) = \int_ {a} ^ {x} \frac {(x - t) ^ {k - 1}}{(k - 1) !} f (t) d t,
$$

a formula due to Cauchy. 

Observe that 

$$
\sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n - 1} A ^ {k} (I - A B) B ^ {k} = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left(A ^ {k} B ^ {k} - A ^ {k + 1} B ^ {k + 1}\right) = I - A ^ {n} B ^ {n}.
$$

Noting that $( I - A B ) ( f ( x ) ) \ = \ f ( a )$ , show that the above telescoping formula gives 

$$
\sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n - 1} \frac {(x - a) ^ {k}}{k !} f ^ {k} (a) = f (x) - \int_ {a} ^ {x} \frac {(x - t) ^ {n - 1}}{(n - 1) !} f ^ {(n)} (t) d t,
$$

which is precisely Taylor’s formula in Cauchy’s form. 

This problem is taken from [261], which contains simple derivations of certain other formulas in analysis. 

4. Here is an interesting approach, using determinants, to Taylor’s formula in Lagrange’s form. 

Let $f ( x ) , \{ f _ { i } ( x ) \} _ { 1 } ^ { n + 2 } ( x ) \}$ be $( n { + } 1 )$ -times continuously diferentiable functions. Then 

$$
\left| \begin{array}{c c c c} f (x) & f _ {1} (x) & \dots & f _ {n + 2} (x) \\ f (0) & f _ {1} (0) & \dots & f _ {n + 2} (0) \\ f ^ {\prime} (0) & f _ {1} ^ {\prime} (0) & \dots & f _ {n + 2} ^ {\prime} (0) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \dots & \vdots \\ f ^ {(n)} (0) & f _ {1} ^ {(n)} (0) & \dots & f _ {n + 2} ^ {(n)} (0) \\ f ^ {(n + 1)} (h) & f _ {1} ^ {(n + 1)} (h) & \dots & f _ {n + 2} ^ {(n + 1)} (h) \end{array} \right| = 0
$$

for some $h$ strictly between 0 and x. To prove this, consider x as a constant and let $D ^ { ( i ) } ( h )$ denote the function of h by replacing the last row of the determinant with $f ^ { ( i ) } ( h ) , f _ { 1 } ^ { ( i ) } ( h ) , \dots , f _ { n + 2 } ^ { ( i ) } ( h )$ 

(a) Show that the derivative of $D ^ { ( i ) } ( h )$ with respect to h is $D ^ { ( i + 1 ) } ( h )$ for $i = 0 , 1 , \ldots , n .$ , and the determinant above is $D ^ { ( n + 1 ) } ( h )$ 

(b) Show that $D ^ { ( 0 ) } ( 0 ) = 0 \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } D ^ { ( 0 ) } ( x ) = 0 .$ 

(c) Use Rolle’s theorem to prove the existence of $h _ { 1 }$ strictly between 0 and x such that $D ^ { ( 1 ) } ( h _ { 1 } ) = 0$ . Also, show that $D ^ { ( 1 ) } ( 0 ) = 0$ . Use Rolle’s theorem again to prove the existence of $h _ { 2 }$ strictly between 0 and $h _ { 1 }$ such that $D ^ { ( 2 ) } ( h _ { 2 } ) = 0$ 

(d) Continue in this fashion to show that there exists a point h strictly between 0 and x such that $D ^ { ( n + 1 ) } ( h ) = 0$ 

As an application, show that there exists a point h strictly between 0 and x such that 

$$
\left| \begin{array}{c c c c c c c} f (x) & 1 & \frac {x}{1 !} & \frac {x ^ {2}}{2 !} & \dots & \frac {x ^ {n}}{n !} & \frac {x ^ {n + 1}}{(n + 1) !} \\ f (0) & 1 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ f ^ {\prime} (0) & 0 & 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots & \dots & \vdots & \vdots \\ f ^ {(n)} (0) & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 1 & 0 \\ f ^ {(n + 1)} (h) & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right| = 0,
$$

and that the above determinant is 

$$
f (x) - f (0) - f ^ {\prime} (0) x - \frac {f ^ {\prime \prime} (0)}{2} x ^ {2} - \dots - \frac {f ^ {(n)} (0)}{n !} x ^ {n} - \frac {f ^ {(n + 1)} (h)}{(n + 1) !} x ^ {n + 1}.
$$

5. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \to \mathbb { R }$ be a function satisfying the inequality $| f ( x ) | \leq \| x \| ^ { 2 }$ Show that f is Fr´echet diferentiable at 0.

exist, but that f is not Gˆateaux diferentiable at (0, 0).
